title: Hosted TextGen: streaming params & fault recovery demo
summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted text-generation focusing on streaming behavior, key parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and practical retry/idempotency patterns for a healthcare use case. Security questions on PHI/HIPAA, audit logs, and KMS were raised. Agreed next steps: share pilot pricing, security pack, and run a 1-week sandbox smoke test with sample prompts.
action_items: Maya Chen - Send pilot pricing sheet and brief on Dedicated vs Hosted (incl. burst) - 2026-04-22
Liam O'Neill - Share recommended params & sample prompt set plus console screenshots - 2026-04-21

Start 1-week hosted sandbox with 100k tokens free credit to validate latency and failure modes

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-04-18 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Aurelia VP Product), Ethan Morales (Aurelia Eng Lead), Sofia Grant (Aurelia Security), Tom Lee (Aurelia Data Eng)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood Inference. Quick intros?
[00:07] Priya: Hi, Priya Rao, VP Product at Aurelia Health. We're looking at using gen models for intake summarization and triage.
[00:14] Ethan: Ethan here, engineering lead. We'll handle integration and want to understand streaming and retries.
[00:20] Sofia: Sofia, security. HIPAA questions up front.
[00:24] Tom: Tom, data eng. I'll be doing the ETL and thinking about PII redaction.
[00:29] Liam: Liam O'Neill, solutions engineer at Redwood — I'll do the live demo and walk through parameters and failure recovery patterns.

[00:40] Maya: Great. Agenda: short overview, live textgen demo (streaming), tune params, talk retries/backoff and idempotency, then security/Qs, and next steps.

[01:12] Liam: I'll share my screen — starting with the Redwood Console, but the same APIs are available via REST/SDKs. The endpoint we'll use is the Hosted text-generation endpoint, chat-style prompts are supported too.

[01:35] Liam: Quick note: streaming means we flush tokens as they're generated. For interactive UIs this gets you visible partial results earlier. But streaming is slightly more sensitive to network interruptions, so we pair it with idempotency keys and resume semantics.

[02:03] Tom: Resume semantics — do you mean you can continue a stream after a drop?
[02:07] Liam: Short answer: not resume the exact TCP stream, but we provide deterministic token offsets and KV cache hints so you can re-request with the same idempotency key and the server will continue from the last committed point for many model variants. There's an internal stuff — sometimes the docs call it "KV cache checkpointing" — and apologies if transcripts later call it KV cash.

[02:45] Priya: Important for us because patient intake flows are long and we want partial summary as agents type.

[03:01] Liam: Totally. Let me run a short prompt: "Summarize the following patient intake notes and highlight allergies, medications, and urgent flags. Keep under 100 tokens and preserve PHI tokenization for our auditability demo."

[03:22] Liam: Using temperature=0.0, top_p=0.8, max_tokens=120; also turning on streaming.

[03:36] [03:36] -- demo output begins (stream chunks) --
[03:40] Liam (screen read): "Patient is a 45-year-old female presenting with chest pain..." (stream continues)

[04:05] Priya: That looks clean, though we'd want stricter PII handling. Can Redwood redact or log-only?
[04:12] Maya: We provide configurable masking at ingestion and can route logs to your VPC for storage. For hosted we offer options: do not log full payloads, store only metadata, or ship encrypted audit logs to your KMS.

[04:34] Sofia: How does KMS integration look? We need BYOK for PHI.

[04:38] Liam: We support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). In private deployments it's standard; in hosted we can integrate your cloud KMS for encrypting stored artifacts and audit exports. I'll attach the KMS doc.

[05:06] Ethan: Back to streaming — what are practical defaults? We worry about hallucination if we set temp high.

[05:12] Liam: For deterministic extraction (like summarization / slot filling) we recommend temperature 0 to 0.2, top_p 0.7-0.95 depending on model, max_tokens bounded tightly. For creative assists (email drafts) temp 0.6-0.9. For cost/latency, reducing max_tokens and using prefix caching reduces token spend. Our Optimize tool suggests quantization or batching changes if throughput is high.

[05:45] Priya: Can you show failure modes? Specifically: what happens if the client times out mid-stream?

[05:51] Liam: Sure. I'll simulate a dropped connection.

[06:03] [06:03] -- simulated drop --
[06:10] Liam: When the client reconnects with the same idempotency key we created for this request, the server can replay the last committed tokens and either continue generating or return a completed response depending on model compatibility. If not compatible, we fallback to a compatible variant and indicate via response metadata that a variant fallback occurred.

[06:35] Tom: Is there an audit trail showing the fallback?
[06:39] Liam: Yes — the Console shows per-request model, latency, token counts, and any fallback events. You can export traces and the token-level cost breakdown.

[06:58] Priya: Timeline and SLA? We're evaluating whether Hosted is acceptable or we need Dedicated or Private.

[07:05] Maya: Hosted is fastest to ship; SLA for Dedicated is stronger (we can do committed throughput). Many customers start on Hosted, then move to Dedicated if they need fixed latency/throughput. Private deployment is available for air-gapped or strict-regulated workflows. We'll send a comparison chart.

[07:33] Ethan: For Hosted, any rate limits that will block us during pilot?

[07:38] Maya: For pilot we'll provision burst capacity and raise default rate limits for your sandbox. Production rate limits are configurable with Reserved capacity.

[08:02] Liam: Now I'll show some code snippets — first the REST call for streaming. (reads) POST /v1/generate with stream=true, idempotency-key header, body includes prompt, temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences. If you want deterministic behavior, include stop tokens and set temperature to 0.

[08:35] Ethan: For idempotency, do you require a unique key per user or per request?

[08:39] Liam: Per request — an idempotency key maps to a logical generation. If you re-send the same key, we return the same generation or continue if incomplete. Keys expire after 24 hours by default; enterprise options can extend that.

[09:02] Sofia: That 24-hour window — we need to map to our retention and audit policies. Can that be shortened or extended?

[09:08] Liam: Yes, configurable via policy. For PHI we suggest shorter retention for raw inputs and longer retention for anonymized transcripts if needed for QA.

[09:30] Priya: You mentioned Optimize — can it recommend param changes automatically?

[09:34] Liam: Yes, Optimize analyzes token distribution and latency traces and suggests batching sizes, caching prefixes, and quantization levels for your workload. For example, it might suggest enabling our prefix cache for the intake form so repeated prompts are cheaper and faster.

[09:58] Tom: We have multi-part prompts where the prompt body gets gradually appended as users type. Does prefix caching help?

[10:05] Liam: Exactly — prefix caching stores KV caches for common prefixes. If the prefix is identical across requests, subsequent calls can reuse the cache and avoid re-computing from scratch, cutting latency and cost. Note: compatibility depends on model architecture and quantization.

[10:34] Priya: Could you show token-level cost and latency in the Console?

[10:38] Liam: Yep. (switches to Console) Here is a per-request trace: tokens_in, tokens_out, model, latency_ms, cost_estimate. We also surface a token counter in real time for streaming sessions.

[11:05] [11:05] -- short pause for screen navigation --
[11:28] Priya: Does console show security events or redaction?

[11:32] Liam: We show redaction settings per API key, and audit logs for requests. For hosted, you can choose to write full logs to our encrypted storage or forward them to your S3 in your VPC.

[11:55] Sofia: About HIPAA — do you sign BAAs?

[11:59] Maya: Redwood offers a BAA for enterprise customers with Private or Dedicated deployments; hosted BAAs are handled case-by-case. We'll include our security pack — SOC2 report, BAA terms, and KMS integration notes.

[12:25] Ethan: One more technical: if we enable streaming and a message hits the stop sequence early, do you still charge for the remainder of the token budget?

[12:31] Liam: You are only charged for tokens generated, so if the model stops early due to stop sequence, you pay for tokens emitted. However if you reserved max_tokens for the call in certain Dedicated plans, accounting may differ; we can clarify in the pricing doc.

[12:58] Priya: Can you show a retry pattern for the SDK?

[13:02] Liam: Sure. Best practice: implement exponential backoff with jitter for 429/5xx, and include idempotency keys to avoid double-processing. For streaming scenarios, we suggest a short retry where the client reconnects and uses the same key; the server will either replay last committed chunks or continue. If the server fallbacked to a different model, we surface that via x-model-variant header.

[13:38] Tom: And what about partial writes? If we get half a summary saved to DB, how do we enforce exactly-once?

[13:44] Liam: Use the idempotency key as the primary key in your DB transaction. The pattern is: send request with key, stream response to temp buffer; on final commit, store under that key. If retry occurs, you can detect that the key exists and skip re-apply.

[14:06] Priya: That helps. Could you also show a short end-to-end demo where we change temperature and see the output differences?

[14:12] Liam: Yep — two quick runs. First temp=0.0, top_p=0.8, then temp=0.8, top_p=0.95, same prompt.

[14:36] [14:36] -- stream A (temp=0.0) --
[14:40] Liam (screen read): "Allergies: Penicillin. Meds: Lisinopril... urgent flag: chest pain, ER referral recommended."

[15:10] [15:10] -- stream B (temp=0.8) --
[15:14] Liam (screen read): "Sounds like chest pain that could be cardiac; patient mentions history of hypertension; consider immediate evaluation; note allergy to penicillin; otherwise meds include... (longer phrasing)"

[15:42] Priya: Good demo of deterministic vs creative. We'll keep extraction deterministic.

[15:55] Sofia: One more on governance — can we limit models by role? Devs use higher-temp models, but production pipelines must use locked-down variants.

[16:03] Liam: Yup — RBAC per API key and per-route model pinning. You can restrict which models a key can call and require approval for model upgrades.

[16:30] Ethan: Latency numbers? For typical 512-token responses what are p50/p95 on your hosted infra?

[16:36] Liam: For the medium-size models we showed, p50 ~120ms per token once KV cache warmed, p95 ~450-800ms depending on burst; for larger models expect higher. Our Console shows these stats per model.

[17:00] Tom: For our expected throughput — ~200 concurrent sessions — do you recommend Dedicated?

[17:06] Maya: Likely a good fit for Dedicated or Reserved capacity; Optimize can simulate cost/latency tradeoffs. We'll model your expected QPS in the pilot.

[17:30] Priya: Security again — SSO and SCIM for user management?

[17:36] Maya: Yes, SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported. We'll enable SSO for the Console trial.

[17:50] [17:50] -- brief side conversation, small crosstalk --
[18:12] Priya: Are there any hidden gotchas for streaming and retries we should watch for?

[18:19] Liam: A few: 1) idempotency key scoping — don't reuse keys across different logical requests; 2) watch stop sequences that might prematurely cut off expected structured output; 3) ensure your client has appropriate socket timeouts and reconnect logic; 4) be careful with prefix caching when you aggressively quantize models — sometimes currency rounding in quantized kernels can change tokenization edge cases.

[18:52] Tom: "currency rounding"? Did you mean "kernel rounding"?

[18:55] Liam: Right — kernel rounding, my bad.

[19:05] Priya: Anything about cost controls? Token caps per key? Alerts?

[19:09] Liam: We provide per-key quotas, alerts when thresholds are approached, and the Console has token burn-rate dashboards. Optimize suggestions also include batching to reduce avg per-token cost.

[19:30] Priya: For the sandbox, we want a small dataset of prompts to validate hallucination rates. Can Redwood help with evaluation harnesses?

[19:37] Liam: Yes — we provide a small eval toolkit and can run regression checks against your prompt set and track quality metrics. We'll show how to link evaluations into the Console for ongoing alerts.

[19:58] Sofia: Any legal constraints around storing prompts that include PHI?

[20:03] Maya: For PHI you should use Private or Dedicated for final production; for initial exploration we can do hosted with strict masking and BAA negotiation. We'll follow up with legal.

[20:28] Ethan: Could you give an example of an idempotency header in code?

[20:32] Liam: Sure, example: headers: { "Idempotency-Key": "aurelia-intake-20260418-xyz123" } and include that same value on retries.

[20:45] [20:45] -- short demo showing header placement in SDK snippet --
[21:02] Priya: How long do model variants persist if you pin a version? We want to pin to avoid regressions.

[21:07] Liam: You can pin to model version (we surface version hashes); pinned versions remain available—depending on the model lifecycle policy—usually for 90 days past deprecation notice, but enterprise contracts can extend that. Pinning also helps with A/B rollouts.

[21:32] Tom: If we need on-prem eventually, how much work is it?

[21:36] Maya: Depends on your infra. We have a private package and orchestration layer for VPC/on-prem installs. Typical project length: 4-12 weeks including security review and data-plane networking.

[21:58] Priya: Ok let's talk timeline for pilot. We want to onboard engineers next week.

[22:04] Maya: We'll provision a sandbox account, bump rate limits, and provide 100k tokens of free credit to run the smoke tests. Liam will share prompt set templates.

[22:18] [22:18] -- small interruption, connectivity checking --
[22:45] Priya: Any final questions from Aurelia?

[22:52] Sofia: Just one — can audit logs be pushed to our SIEM in near-real-time?

[22:58] Liam: Yes — event webhook or Kinesis/SQS connector into your VPC. We'll include a connector guide.

[23:20] Maya: Great. I'll recap next steps in chat.

[23:27] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks all.

[23:33] [23:33] -- end of main demo portion; remaining time was Q&A and logistics --

[30:00] [30:00] -- Q&A picks up: pricing, legal contacts, pilot metrics definition --
[30:12] Priya: For pilot success metrics: latency p95 < 1s token steady state, hallucination rate < 2% on extraction fields, cost per completed intake < $0.10. Can Redwood help measure?

[30:30] Liam: Yes we'll instrument those metrics and add to the trial dashboard.

[35:00] [35:00] -- longer discussion on security details; Sofia and Maya exchange emails --

[42:00] [42:00] -- final wrap-up --
[42:05] Maya: Quick recap: Redwood to send pilot pricing and Hosted vs Dedicated comparison, Liam to send params and sample prompts and connector docs, security to exchange BAA and KMS notes. We'll schedule sandbox kickoff with engineering.

[42:35] Priya: We'll confirm internal stakeholders and pick a date. Thanks for the demo.

[42:45] Ethan: Thank you, that was helpful.

[42:50] Sofia: Thanks.

[43:00] Maya: Okay, closing now.

[43:05] -- call ends --
